## The Collective Review

**Code owners summoned:** The Database Architect (two new financial tables)
**Rotating specialist:** none (one code owner fired, and a two-commit repo has little history to weigh)

**The Scope Hawk:** "The fixes below add about 20 lines to a 15-line file, which is still one commit. Cut `invoice_items_sku_idx` unless a query for it is coming, because `invoices_for` at `db.py:5` is the only query in the repo and never touches `sku`. Skip a products table, status enum, tax fields and down migration, since nothing needs them yet. The unused `import psycopg` and missing type hints in `db.py` belong in another commit."

**The Craftsperson:** "Nothing verifies this migration: the repo has no tests or migration runner, only `README.md`, `db.py` and `001_users.sql`. `qty INT NOT NULL` accepts `0` and `-5`, so add `CHECK (qty > 0)`. `total_cents` accepts negatives too, so decide whether credit notes make those legal. The file has three statements and no `BEGIN`, so under plain `psql -f` a failure on the last one leaves both tables behind and a rerun fails on `already exists`."

**The Performance Engineer:** "`invoices_for` filters on `user_id`, and Postgres doesn't index foreign keys automatically, so every call scans all of `invoices`. Loading an invoice's items has the same problem because `invoice_items.invoice_id` has no index. The one index this file does add serves no current query. `SELECT *` at `db.py:5` also pulls `raw_payload` on every list call: at an assumed 10 KB per payload, a user with 100 invoices costs 1 MB per call."

**The Readability Advocate:** "The names mostly work: `total_cents` carries its unit, and the style matches `001_users.sql`. `raw_payload` is the exception, because it doesn't say which system sent it or whether `NULL` is normal. A `COMMENT ON COLUMN` would answer both."

**The User Advocate:** "A user can't get a useful invoice list from this. `invoices` has no date of any kind and `invoices_for` has no `ORDER BY`, so nothing says when an invoice was created or how to sort the list. Line items show `sku` and `qty` with no price, so nobody can see how `total_cents` was reached."

**The Database Architect:** "Neither table has `created_at`, `updated_at` or `deleted_at`, which breaks the audit-column rule; `001_users.sql` has all three. No `updated_at` trigger exists anywhere in the repo, so this migration has to create the function. Once `deleted_at` exists, `db.py:5` needs `AND deleted_at IS NULL`, or soft-deleted invoices keep coming back. Add `unit_price_cents` to `invoice_items`, because without it `total_cents` can't be reconciled and a later price change can't be reconstructed. `raw_payload` suggests invoices come from an API. If so, make it `NOT NULL` so a payload can't go missing, and add `external_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE` so a retried delivery can't create a duplicate invoice. The default `NO ACTION` foreign keys are right, since they block hard-deleting a user who has invoices."

**The Adult:** "Don't commit this yet. The basic shape is fine, and the 80/20 is three changes:

1. **Audit columns (required):** Add all three columns to both tables, plus the `updated_at` trigger. Update `db.py:5` to filter on `deleted_at IS NULL`, add `ORDER BY created_at DESC`, and list its columns explicitly so it stops fetching `raw_payload`.
2. **Indexes (required):** Add indexes on `invoices (user_id)` and `invoice_items (invoice_id)`, and drop the `sku` index unless a query for it is coming.
3. **Data you can't easily recover later (before the first real rows):** Add `unit_price_cents`. If invoices come from an external API, also make `raw_payload` `NOT NULL` and add `external_id`.

The Hawk wins on products, status and tax; the Architect wins on anything unrecoverable. `CHECK (qty > 0)` and `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` are cheap enough to include, though skip the `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` if your runner already wraps each migration. Currency can wait if you only bill in one, since adding a column with a default later is cheap. Attach the trigger to `users` in a follow-up `003` rather than editing the committed `001`. There's no need to split this up."

I didn't change or run anything, so this SQL hasn't been applied to Postgres. Once the fixes are in, this checks the migrations against a scratch database (it needs local Postgres, and I haven't run it):

```sh
createdb mig_check && { psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d mig_check -f migrations/001_users.sql -f migrations/002_invoices.sql; dropdb mig_check; }
```

Rough cost: at least $0.21, from the session budget meter before this reply.
